# Change Plan — Adding a Field to `orders-ledger` Records

**Prepared for:** the owner of the `orders-ledger` stream
**Status:** executable as written, subject to the Open items at the end
**Date prepared:** 2026-08-10

---

## 1. What this plan covers

Adding one new field to the records carried on the `orders-ledger` stream, from first proposal through to the field being live and the change formally closed.

The specific field — its name, type, semantics, nullability, source of the value, and whether existing records are to be backfilled with it — is not recorded on this platform and was not supplied with the request. Every step below is written to be executed against whatever that field turns out to be; the places where the field's own properties change the answer are called out inline and listed in Open items.

## 2. The standing of this stream, and why it constrains you

`orders-ledger` carries the order lifecycle records every revenue report is built from. It is a **governed-tier** stream: its records feed the statutory accounts, and — in the runbook's own words — everything about how it changes is bound by *Governed Tier Obligations* **rather than by the producing team's own judgment**.

Three consequences shape this entire plan:

1. **The change is classified before any work begins**, and the owner cannot waive a classification.
2. **The producing team does not announce anything directly.** Consumer-facing notice is issued centrally.
3. **Timing is not the producing team's to decide.** It also observes the finance organization's close calendar.

## 3. Classification — do this before any work begins

Under the *Change Class Directory*, class **RB-7** covers incompatible changes to a stream's record shape, and the directory enumerates the triggering changes explicitly as "a field added, renamed, retyped or removed." **A field addition is named in that list.** Plan for RB-7.

What RB-7 obliges:

- **17 business days of advance notice to consumers before the change is applied**, counted in the *consuming teams'* working calendar.
- The notice **runs from the day the announcement is actually delivered**, not from the day it is drafted, approved, or submitted.
- **The class does not shorten for changes the producer considers small.** Compatibility is judged from the consumer's side.

The directory also says that compatible additions and operational-only changes carry lighter classes, which owe an announcement but no waiting period. Do not treat that as a self-service exit: the tie-break rule is that **when in doubt between two classes, the heavier one applies until the owner of the consuming side agrees otherwise in writing.** So the only route from RB-7 to a lighter class is a written agreement from the consuming-side owner(s), obtained in advance and filed with the change. Absent that, execute at RB-7.

The material does not say which role or body assigns the classification, only that the owner cannot waive it. See Open items.

## 4. Approvals this change needs

| # | Approval | Who gives it | When | Source of the rule |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Classification of the change (RB-7 assumed) | Not stated — the owner may not waive it | Before any work begins | Governed Tier Obligations; Change Class Directory |
| 2 | Written agreement to a lighter class, **only if** you intend to argue the addition is compatible | The owner of the consuming side | Before work begins, alongside classification | Change Class Directory |
| 3 | Approval of the new schema version at registration | Not stated — the register entry records "who approved it" | Before any producer writes the new shape | Schema Version Register |
| 4 | Written exception to the QW-4 quiet window, **only if** the change cannot wait for statement sign-off | The controller's office | Before applying during QW-4; recorded as a finding in the close report | Company Close Calendar |
| 5 | Waiver of the waiting period for individual consumers whose declared fields are untouched | The announcing owner's discretion — see §6 caveat | During the notice period | Consumer Agreement Ledger |
| 6 | **EG-24 approval**, only if any copy of stream output leaves the platform (e.g. a sample payload sent to a consumer outside the platform for testing) | Not stated; the approval must name receiving party, purpose, and deletion date, and cite a covering instrument from the legal office's directory | Filed **before** the copy is made | Off-platform Copy Policy |
| 7 | **AT-12 attestation** closing the change | The producing service's named owner, personally | After the change is live and the first full settlement has passed | Attestation Procedure |

Approvals 2, 4 and 6 are conditional. Approvals 1, 3 and 7 are unavoidable for this change.

## 5. Rules that constrain when the change may be applied

**Registration precedes writing.** A new version is registered *before any producer writes it*. A record shape that reaches the stream unregistered is an **incident, not a shortcut**. There is no "ship it and register after."

**CM-3 compatibility.** The orders and settlement streams sit in compatibility mode **CM-3, the strictest**: a new version must be **readable by every consumer of the previous one without a code change**. Every proposed version is checked against the stream's declared mode at registration time. This is the substantive technical bar for the new field — it is checked at registration, so a field design that fails CM-3 fails before you write a line of producer code.

**The 17-business-day RB-7 clock**, running from actual delivery of the announcement, in the consuming teams' working calendar.

**QW-4 quiet window.** The stretch from journal cutoff to statement sign-off is the QW-4 quiet window. During QW-4, systems whose figures flow into the statements are left as they are; production alterations wait until the books are signed. `orders-ledger` feeds the statutory accounts, so it is squarely in scope. Exceptions are granted in writing by the controller's office and are **treated as findings in the close report** — an exception is a cost, not a neutral option. The current period's cutoff times and the window's standing are published on the finance group's internal page each period; they are not recorded here (Open items).

**The settlement cadence.** The stream settles during the overnight window and its lag is reviewed each morning. This matters twice: pick an application point that respects that cadence, and note that attestation cannot be filed until the first full settlement after the change has passed.

**Owner vacancy.** The AT-12 signature cannot be delegated below the service's named owner, and **a vacancy in that role suspends changes rather than the attestation.** If the stream has no named owner at any point, this change stops until one is in place.

## 6. What the consumers are owed

Consumers are defined by the **Consumer Agreement Ledger**. Each consuming team registers a **CA-9 agreement** per stream it reads, naming the consuming service, its owner, and **the fields it depends on**. Registration is a condition of read access and is also **the notice boundary**: announcements go to registered consumers, and a team that never registered is owed nothing, however long it has been reading.

What is owed, in order:

1. **An AN-5 bulletin.** Governed-stream changes are announced as an AN-5 bulletin, issued centrally so that no consumer's notice depends on which team is making the change. **You do not announce this yourself** — you submit it to the announcing function.
2. **Delivery to every consumer the stream's agreement ledger lists.** Not "the teams you know about" — the ledger's list.
3. **Posting against the stream's register entry.** The bulletin is posted against the register entry, and **the register copy is authoritative when a delivered copy and the register disagree.** Confirm the posting, not just the send.
4. **17 business days between delivery and application** (per §3).
5. **An agreement review.** Agreements are reviewed when a stream's shape changes. Walk each CA-9's declared fields against the change.
6. **Filing with delivery evidence.** Issued bulletins are corporate correspondence filed under series **RR-21** — issued circulars and bulletins — **with their delivery evidence at the time of issue**. Filing is part of issuing, not an afterthought. Retention length is what the records directory lists for RR-21, and disposal is reviewed by the records office, not by you or the announcing team.

**Caveat on the waiting-period discretion.** The Consumer Agreement Ledger says a consumer whose declared fields are untouched by a change "may be notified without being waited for, at the announcing owner's discretion." A pure field addition touches no existing declared field, so on its face this discretion is available for most or all consumers. It sits in tension with RB-7's rule that the class "does not shorten for changes the producer considers small" and that compatibility is judged from the consumer's side. The material does not resolve which governs. **Execute the full 17 business days unless the announcing owner explicitly exercises that discretion in writing per consumer, and record the reasoning.** Flagged in Open items.

## 7. Step-by-step execution

### Phase A — Classify and scope (before any work)

- **A1.** Write up the change: the field, its type, its meaning, its source, and how it behaves for records where no value exists. Nothing downstream can be checked without this.
- **A2.** Obtain the classification. Assume RB-7. Do not begin engineering work before the classification exists — the obligation is that every change is classified *before any work begins*.
- **A3.** If, and only if, you intend to run at a lighter class, obtain the consuming-side owner's written agreement first. Otherwise skip.
- **A4.** Confirm the stream has a named owner in post (see the vacancy rule in §5). If not, stop here.
- **Exit condition:** a classification exists, and the owner role is filled.

### Phase B — Register the version

- **B1.** Pull the current registered version of `orders-ledger` from the Schema Version Register — the register is the authoritative record of what shape the records have ever had.
- **B2.** Draft the proposed new version, adding the field to the current registered shape.
- **B3.** Check it against **CM-3**: every consumer of the previous version must be able to read the new version **without a code change**. Use the CA-9 declared-field lists as the population of consumers to check against. This is checked at registration regardless, so failing it here saves a rejection.
- **B4.** Submit for registration. The entry will carry the version, the classification from A2, and who approved it.
- **Exit condition:** the new version is registered and approved. **No producer writes the new shape before this point** — an unregistered shape reaching the stream is an incident.

### Phase C — Consumer review

- **C1.** Read the stream's CA-9 agreements. For each registered consumer, record: service, owner, declared fields.
- **C2.** Perform the agreement review that a shape change triggers. Note which consumers' declared fields are untouched (for a pure addition, expected to be all of them) and which, if any, are affected.
- **C3.** Decide — and write down — whether you are exercising the "notify without waiting" discretion for any consumer, per the caveat in §6. Default is no.
- **Exit condition:** a per-consumer notice-and-wait list.

### Phase D — Announce

- **D1.** Submit the AN-5 bulletin to the central announcing function. Content should carry, at minimum, the registered version, the classification, the field being added, the intended application date, and what consumers need to do (for a CM-3-clean addition: nothing, but say so).
- **D2.** Confirm delivery to **every** consumer on the ledger's list, and capture the delivery evidence.
- **D3.** Confirm the bulletin is posted against the stream's register entry, and that the posted copy matches what was delivered — the register copy wins in a disagreement, so a mismatch is yours to fix now, not after.
- **D4.** Confirm the bulletin and its delivery evidence are filed under RR-21 at the time of issue.
- **Exit condition:** delivered, posted, filed. **Record the actual delivery date — the RB-7 clock starts here.**

### Phase E — Wait

- **E1.** Count 17 business days from the actual delivery date, in the consuming teams' working calendar.
- **E2.** In parallel, build and test the producer change against the registered version. Building during the notice period is not an application of the change; only the production alteration is.
- **E3.** If testing requires any stream output to leave the platform, obtain an EG-24 approval first, naming receiving party, purpose, and deletion date, and citing a covering instrument from the legal office's directory. An approval missing any of the three is returned unactioned, and a transfer with no instrument to cite does not proceed.
- **Exit condition:** the 17 business days have elapsed.

### Phase F — Schedule against the close calendar

- **F1.** Check the current period's journal cutoff and statement sign-off dates on the finance group's internal page, and the QW-4 window's current standing.
- **F2.** If the intended application date falls outside QW-4, proceed.
- **F3.** If it falls inside QW-4, either move it past statement sign-off (the default and cheaper path), or obtain a written exception from the controller's office, accepting that it will be recorded as a finding in the close report.
- **F4.** Choose an application point consistent with the stream's overnight settlement and morning lag review.
- **Exit condition:** an application slot that is outside QW-4 or covered by a written exception.

### Phase G — Apply

- **G1.** Apply the producer change so that records begin carrying the field, in the shape registered in Phase B and no other.
- **G2.** Watch the overnight settlement and the morning lag review through the first full settlement after the change.
- **G3.** Verify the records now flowing match the registered version exactly, and that no consumer-visible field was dropped in the process — these are the things you will personally attest to.
- **Exit condition:** the first full settlement after the change has passed and been checked.

### Phase H — Attest and close

- **H1.** The producing service's **named owner personally** files form **AT-12**, once the change is live and the first full settlement has passed. It cannot be delegated below the named owner.
- **H2.** The form states three things — verify each before signing: the records now flowing match the registered version; no consumer-visible field was dropped along the way; the announced scope is the delivered scope. If the delivered change differs in any way from what the AN-5 bulletin described, the third statement is not true, and the divergence must be resolved before the form is filed.
- **H3.** File it. An unattested change stays open in the tier's books and is raised at every review until the form is filed, however long it has been live.
- **Exit condition:** AT-12 filed. The change is closed.

## 8. Records this change produces

| Record | Where it lives | Who controls it |
|---|---|---|
| Classification of the change | Carried on the register entry | Not stated |
| New schema version + approver | Schema Version Register | The register |
| AN-5 bulletin + delivery evidence | Filed under series RR-21; posted against the register entry | Records office (disposal), announcing function (issue) |
| CA-9 agreement review outcome | Consumer Agreement Ledger | The ledger |
| Written lighter-class agreement, if any | With the change record | Consuming-side owner |
| QW-4 exception, if any | Controller's office; appears as a finding in the close report | Controller's office |
| EG-24 approval, if any | Filed before the copy is made | Not stated |
| AT-12 attestation | The tier's books | The named owner |

## 9. Conditions that stop or hold the change

- The proposed version fails the **CM-3** check at registration — redesign the field; do not proceed to announcement.
- The **owner role is vacant** — changes are suspended until it is filled; the attestation is not what gets suspended.
- The application date falls in **QW-4** without a written controller's exception.
- Fewer than **17 business days** have elapsed since actual delivery of the bulletin.
- The **delivered bulletin and the register posting disagree** — the register is authoritative; reconcile before applying.
- **Delivered scope diverges from announced scope** — this blocks AT-12, so it must be caught before or at Phase G, not at signing.
- Any producer writes the new shape **before registration** — this is an incident and is handled as one.

1. **The owning team for settlement-recon is not named anywhere on this platform.** Band SB-8 requires notifying "the owning team" at opening, but no recorded page identifies who that is for this job. The settlement-recon runbook refers only to "the job's operators". Resolve before sending the opening notice.

2. **The names on the garnet roster are not recorded.** The route gives roles — platform shift lead, duty manager, head of platform operations — and the roster is explicit that "the roster decides the names", but the current names and contact routes for those roles are not in the retrieved material.
3. **The system in which an IN-28 record is opened is not recorded.** The material names the record type but not the tool, queue, or form used to open one.

4. **The UC-11 update interval is not specified.** The standard says the cadence is whatever the opening notice declared and that it is binding, but records no default or maximum interval for control-failure incidents. The engineer must choose the interval; nothing recorded constrains that choice.

5. **The full notification audience is not enumerated.** The Communications Standard forbids narrowing the audience and requires the closing notice to reach "the full audience", but only the owning team and the platform shift lead are named as the opening notification. Whether the audience is intended to be broader than those two is not stated.

6. **Whether a statutory filing window is currently open, and whether these settlement days are in scope, cannot be determined here.** The Regulatory Filing Calendar page describes how windows work but the window contents are not in the retrieved material. This must be checked directly with the compliance office (§4) — and it is the most time-critical unknown in this document.

7. **The PM-6 due clock is not specified.** The Closure Evidence Standard says the review record is due "on the standard's own clock rather than at closure time", but the Review Record Standard does not state what that clock is.
8. **Who convenes and chairs the review meeting is not recorded.** The PM-6 record carries "the review meeting's outcome", but nothing states who schedules it, who must attend, or by when it is held.

9. **Whether settlement-recon repairs via RP-22 is not stated explicitly.** The Feed Re-run Procedure governs "a nightly feed's bad night" and the settlement-recon runbook does not name RP-22 as its repair path — it says only that a failed pass is re-attempted the following night after the upstream statements refresh. §7.2 is written as the procedure that applies *if* a re-run is used; confirm with the owning team whether re-running the feed is in fact the repair path for this control.

# Incident Handling Document — Settlement-Recon Job, Third Consecutive Failed Night

**Control:** nightly settlement-recon job (agrees the day's settlement records against the processor statements)
**Condition:** three consecutive failed nights, as of 2026-08-10
**Audience:** the on-shift engineer, to be followed as written
**Basis:** the operating standards recorded on this platform; every rule below is cited to the page that owns it

---

## 0. At a glance

| Question | Answer | Owning standard |
|---|---|---|
| What is opened? | An **IN-28 incident record** | Settlement Recon Job Runbook |
| At what severity? | Band **SB-8** | Incident Severity Standard |
| Who is told at opening? | The owning team **and** the platform group's shift lead | Incident Severity Standard |
| How does it escalate? | The **garnet route**: platform shift lead → duty manager → head of platform operations | Escalation Roster |
| On what clocks? | **23 min** (rung 1), **34 min** (rung 2), rung 3 **holds until answered** | Acknowledgment Clock Table |
| What if nobody answers? | Rule **AC-15**: the clock advances the call on its own; the missed rung is recorded as missed, not retried | Acknowledgment Clock Table |
| What is communicated? | Cadence **UC-11**, on the promise made in the opening notice | Incident Communications Standard |
| What allows closure? | A **CE-2 evidence record** — an unassisted scheduled pass with the unagreed days brought current | Closure Evidence Standard |
| What record remains? | A **PM-6 review record**, plus **TL-19** hours entries | Review Record Standard; Worked Hours Ledger Practice |
| Extra obligation | If the failure falls inside a statutory filing window: **form RN-26**, via the compliance office | Regulatory Filing Calendar |

---

## 1. Confirm the trigger before doing anything else

The escalation ladder in this document is driven by a specific threshold, so confirm the threshold is actually met before opening a record at SB-8.

The Settlement Recon Job Runbook sets three tiers:

1. **One failed night** is watched. No record.
2. **Two failed nights** are worked during the day. No record.
3. **A third consecutive failed night** is no longer an operational matter. It opens an IN-28 incident record, *because the unagreed days now span a statement cycle*.

Checks to make before opening:

- [ ] The three failures are **consecutive** nights, not three failures spread across a longer period.
- [ ] Each was a genuine failed pass, leaving the day unagreed — not a clean pass that alerted for another reason. A clean pass is silent.
- [ ] Record the three dates and the specific settlement days left unagreed. You will need this exact list four times over: in the opening notice, in any RN-26, in the CE-2 evidence record, and in the PM-6 timeline.

The runbook notes the job re-attempts a failed pass the following night, after the upstream statements refresh. A third consecutive failure therefore means three refreshed attempts have not cleared the day — this is not a case to wait one more night on.

**The runbook's own scope ends at opening the record honestly.** Severity, notification, escalation, communications and closure are not the job operators' to decide; they belong to the standards cited below.

---

## 2. What is opened, and at what severity

**Open an IN-28 incident record.**

**Assign band SB-8.** The Incident Severity Standard is explicit that a reconciliation or settlement control failing across a statement cycle is band SB-8, that severity is assigned when the record is opened, and that it *belongs to the standard, not to the team that opened it*. You do not have discretion here, and neither does the owning team:

- Do not open this at a lighter band because a fix looks imminent. The lighter bands are for single-night failures and non-control degradations; they notify the owning team only and do not escalate unattended. This condition is neither.
- Do not defer opening the record until someone senior agrees the severity. The band follows from the condition.

Record in the incident, at opening: the control name, the three failed nights, the settlement days left unagreed, the band (SB-8), and the route it escalates on (garnet).

---

## 3. Who has to be told, at opening

Band SB-8 notifies, at opening:

1. **The owning team** for the settlement-recon job.
2. **The platform group's shift lead.**

Notify both. The shift lead is not merely an observer here — the shift lead is the first rung of the garnet route, so this notification also starts the escalation clock described in §5.

> The material on this platform does not name the owning team for settlement-recon. See *Open items*. Resolve the name before you send the opening notice; do not substitute a general engineering channel for the owning team's own notification.

**Separately and in parallel, see §4** — the regulatory obligation is not part of the engineering notification and is not the engineering organization's to schedule.

---

## 4. Regulatory notification — check this early, it is the most time-sensitive item

The Incident Severity Standard states that bands touching settlement controls carry one further obligation, which the engineering organization does not schedule: **when the failure falls inside a statutory filing window, notification follows the Regulatory Filing Calendar, maintained by the compliance office.**

Settlement-recon is a settlement control, so this test applies to this incident. Do it at opening, not at closure.

**Steps:**

1. **Determine whether a statutory filing window is currently open.** Windows are published a year ahead by the compliance office, each naming its filing, its lodgment date, and the list of in-scope arrangements the filing draws on.
2. **Determine whether the settlement arrangement behind these unagreed days is on that window's in-scope list.** If this is not obvious from the published list, ask the compliance office in writing — the office confirms scope questions in writing within a working day.
3. **If the answer is yes, tell the compliance office now, in writing,** with: the control interrupted, the days affected, and the current state of the incident.

**Why the urgency.** Where anything on the in-scope list was interrupted while the filing was being prepared, **form RN-26** is lodged with the filing before the window closes, stating what was interrupted, the days affected, and the basis on which the filed figures stand. The office can only lodge what it has been told while the window is open. Word arriving after lodgment becomes a **correction**, which the regulators treat differently. A day's delay in telling them can convert a routine declaration into a regulatory correction.

**Do not expect the office to chase you.** During a window, the office's attention belongs to the filing, not to new requests. Push the information to them; make the notification, in writing, self-contained.

RN-26 is lodged by the compliance office, not by you. Your obligation is to supply what it must state, in time, and to record in the incident that you did so.

---

## 5. Escalation: the route, the rungs, and the clocks

### 5.1 The route

SB-8 escalates along the **garnet route** (Incident Severity Standard). Severity decides the route; the roster decides the names.

The garnet route climbs (Escalation Roster):

| Rung | Role | Hold time | Behaviour on expiry |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Platform shift lead | **23 minutes** | Advances to rung 2 automatically; rung 1 recorded as missed |
| 2 | Duty manager | **34 minutes** | Advances to rung 3 automatically; rung 2 recorded as missed |
| 3 | Head of platform operations | **Holds until answered** | Nowhere further to climb — it stays here |

The 23- and 34-minute clocks are those the Acknowledgment Clock Table records for the **settlement family of routes**, which is the family this incident sits in. The clocks belong to that table, not to the roster, so a clock change never edits a route — if you are checking the current clock, check the table, not the roster.

### 5.2 How the climb behaves

Governed by **rule AC-15**:

- **An expired clock advances the call to the next rung on its own.** You do not need to decide to escalate; the absence of an acknowledgment escalates for you. Equally, do not sit on an unacknowledged rung past its clock waiting for a reply.
- **A missed rung is recorded as missed, not retried.** Do not loop back to re-page the shift lead once the call has moved to the duty manager. The miss is part of the record.
- **Acknowledging stops the climb at that rung.** Once a rung acknowledges, the escalation rests there.
- **Declining passes it upward immediately, without waiting out the clock.** A decline is faster than a timeout, not slower.
- **A rung that has acknowledged is never skipped.** The ladder is climbed one rung at a time.

### 5.3 Practical notes for the on-shift engineer

- The clock cycle for a completely unanswered escalation is 23 + 34 = **57 minutes** before it reaches the head of platform operations, where it then holds until answered. Plan your first update promise (§6) against that reality.
- **An escalation in flight finishes on the roster it started on.** If the roster is edited while this incident is live, keep climbing the ladder you started on.
- Log, against the incident, for each rung: when it was paged, when the clock expired or was acknowledged or declined, and by whom. §9's review record depends on this being written down at the time.

---

## 6. What is communicated while the incident is open

Governed by the Incident Communications Standard. Control-failure incidents use **cadence UC-11**.

### 6.1 The opening notice

The opening notice must name:

1. **The affected control** — the nightly settlement-recon job.
2. **The days in question** — the three failed nights and the settlement days left unagreed.
3. **When the next update will arrive** — a specific time, not "shortly" or "when we know more".

### 6.2 The cadence is a promise

**An open incident communicates on the cadence its opening notice declared, and the cadence is a promise: missing an update is itself reportable.** Two consequences you must act on:

- **Do not promise a cadence you cannot keep.** The interval you name in the opening notice binds you and everyone who takes the incident over. Choose an interval you can meet during quiet hours, through a shift handover, and while you are heads-down on the actual failure.
- **Every update thereafter either reports progress or re-promises the next time honestly.** "No change; next update at 14:00" is a compliant update. Silence is not, and neither is a re-promise you already know you will miss.

### 6.3 The audience never narrows

**Updates go to the same audience as the opening notice. Narrowing the audience mid-incident is not permitted, however quiet the update.** A no-change update goes to everyone the opening notice went to. Do not drop the shift lead, the duty manager, or anyone else from the distribution because an update seems routine.

Record the opening audience explicitly in the incident at opening, so that whoever holds the incident at 04:00 sends to the same list.

### 6.4 The closing notice

The closing notice is part of the standard too: **it goes to the full audience and names the evidence the closure rests on** — that is, the CE-2 record described in §8. It cannot go out before that record exists and is attached.

---

## 7. Working the incident while it is open

### 7.1 The job keeps running

**The job keeps running on its schedule while the incident is open** (Settlement Recon Job Runbook). Do not disable it to quiet the alerting. Beyond the operational cost, a disabled control destroys the only thing that can close this incident: §8 requires a *scheduled, unassisted pass*, and a quiet night with the control disabled explicitly does not qualify.

### 7.2 Repairing a bad night

Where repair is by re-running a feed, **procedure RP-22** governs (Feed Re-run Procedure):

- **A re-run repairs a bad night by replacing it, never by appending to it.** The affected write-date partitions are replaced whole, under the feed's own prefix.
- **The original write date stays the partition's identity.** A re-run performed days later still lands under the night it repairs, so consumers re-reading the partition see the corrected records where the bad ones were.
- **A re-run that would change a partition's write date is not a re-run.** It is a new feed writing into an old feed's zone, and the layout forbids it.
- **Re-run only after the upstream collectors have drained for the affected window.** Re-running ahead of the upstream repair reproduces the bad night. This matters especially here: the settlement-recon job's own failed passes are re-attempted after the upstream statements refresh, so the upstream state is the thing to check first, every time.

### 7.3 A repair is not a closure

Keep the two apart in your head and in the incident log. A successful re-run or a manually forced pass may bring the days current — but under §8 it cannot close the incident. Closure waits for the *next scheduled, unassisted* pass.

---

## 8. What has to be true before the incident can be closed

Governed by the Closure Evidence Standard: **a control-failure incident closes on evidence, not on silence.**

Closure requires a **CE-2 evidence record** showing all of the following:

- [ ] **The control passed** — a genuine pass, not an absence of alerts.
- [ ] **On its own schedule** — the record must come from the scheduled run itself.
- [ ] **Unassisted** — a manually forced pass does not qualify.
- [ ] **With the previously unagreed days brought current** — the specific days from §1, not merely the current night.

Explicitly disqualifying, per the standard:

- A **manually forced pass**. It does not qualify.
- **A quiet night with the control disabled**. It "qualifies even less" — silence from a disabled control is the opposite of evidence.

**Sequence, which is not optional:** the CE-2 record is **attached to the incident before the closing notice goes out**. Attach first, then notify. The closing notice names the evidence the closure rests on (§6.4), so it has nothing to name until the record is attached.

**One more artifact is owed after closure.** Closing the incident does not discharge it: the PM-6 review record (§9) remains due, **on the Review Record Standard's own clock rather than at closure time**. Do not treat a closed incident as a finished one.

---

## 9. The record the incident has to leave behind

### 9.1 The PM-6 review record

**Every closed control-failure incident files a PM-6 review record** (Review Record Standard). It carries:

1. **A timeline of the nights in question** — the three failed nights, what was attempted each night, the escalation as it actually climbed (including any rung recorded as missed under AC-15), each communication sent, and the passes that produced the CE-2 evidence.
2. **The originating conditions as they are actually understood.** As actually understood — if the cause is partly unresolved, the record says so. A tidy narrative that outruns the evidence is not what the standard asks for.
3. **The corrections that will be made, with a named owner for each.** This is a hard gate: **a record whose corrections have no owner is returned to the incident's owner rather than filed.** A team name is not an owner; name a person for each correction before submitting.
4. **The review meeting's outcome.**

**Owned corrections are tracked to completion** — filing the record starts that tracking, it does not end it.

**Where it is filed:** against the incident, **and referenced from the control's own operating notes** — here, the Settlement Recon Job Runbook (`mcp:knowledge_page:kp_f396db6f-11ee-428e-8648-eedbe560e2b3`). Both. The purpose is stated in the standard: *so the next operator to meet the same failure finds what the last one learned.* An incident-only filing fails that purpose, because the next operator at 02:00 reads the runbook, not the incident archive.

### 9.2 TL-19 hours — do this before the record is filed

The review record also closes the people side. **Hours spent on the nights in question are entered under the Worked Hours Ledger Practice before the record is filed,** because the workforce office's ledger closes on its own rhythm whether or not the review is done.

For each person who worked these nights:

- **Ordinary working days need no action** — they flow into the ledger from badge records.
- **Hours worked outside the working day are entered by hand under code TL-19,** with **the date and a one-line purpose**, **before the payroll cutoff of the following week.** Three consecutive nights of settlement-recon failures will mostly be exactly these hours.
- **An unentered line lapses.** The ledger closes with payroll and a late claim reopens nothing. This deadline can fall well before the review meeting, which is precisely why the standard puts the entries ahead of the filing.
- Entered TL-19 hours accrue toward time off in lieu, at the rate the employment terms set; the balance is visible beside leave in the workforce portal.
- **If a period has already closed**, it is no longer a ledger entry but a **payroll correction**: the payroll administrators apply it on the following run and it adjusts pay, never the closed ledger itself. Questions about a closed period go to the workforce office in writing and are answered against the ledger as it closed.

---

## 10. Ordered checklist

**At opening (minute zero):**
1. Confirm three *consecutive* failed nights; list the nights and the unagreed settlement days. (§1)
2. Open the IN-28 record at band **SB-8**. (§2)
3. Notify the **owning team** and the **platform group's shift lead**. (§3)
4. Send the **opening notice**: control, days in question, time of next update. Record the audience list in the incident. (§6.1)
5. Start the **garnet** escalation at rung 1; note the page time. (§5)
6. Run the **filing-window test**; if in scope, notify the compliance office **in writing**, now. (§4)

**Through the first hour:**
7. At **+23 min** unacknowledged → the call advances to the duty manager; log rung 1 as missed. (§5.2)
8. At **+57 min** unacknowledged → the call advances to the head of platform operations and holds until answered. (§5.2)
9. Confirm the job is still running on schedule; do not disable it. (§7.1)

**For the duration:**
10. Send every update on the promised cadence, to the full original audience, reporting progress or re-promising honestly. (§6.2, §6.3)
11. Repair under **RP-22** if re-running: replace partitions whole, keep the original write date, only after upstream has drained. (§7.2)
12. Keep a contemporaneous log of pages, acknowledgments, misses, and notices — the PM-6 timeline depends on it. (§9.1)

**To close:**
13. Wait for a **scheduled, unassisted** pass that brings the unagreed days current. (§8)
14. Attach the **CE-2** record to the incident. (§8)
15. Send the **closing notice** to the full audience, naming that evidence. (§6.4)

**After closure:**

17. Hold the review; write the **PM-6** record with a named owner on every correction. (§9.1)
18. File it against the incident **and** reference it from the Settlement Recon Job Runbook. (§9.1)
19. Track the owned corrections to completion. (§9.1)

# Onboarding Document — `invoice-adjustments` Nightly Feed

**Status:** onboarding specification, prepared 2026-08-10
**Model feed:** `parcel-events` — this feed is to be operated exactly like it

## 1. Scope and how to read this document

`invoice-adjustments` is a new nightly feed to be stood up and operated on the same terms as the `parcel-events` feed. `parcel-events` is explicitly the feed other nightly feeds are stood up from, and almost nothing that makes it operable lives in its own runbook — everything operable lives in the platform-wide standards it follows. Onboarding `invoice-adjustments` therefore means enrolling it in that same chain of standards, not writing a bespoke set of rules for it.

The standards that apply, in the order this document covers them:

| Area | Standard | Rule identifier |
|---|---|---|
| Feed and output naming | Feed Naming Standard | FN-13 |
| Where output lands, how organized | Landing Zone Layout | LZ-14 |
| Storage registration and output lifetime | Storage Tier Register | ST-16 |
| Capacity behind the registration | Procurement Commitment Ledger | PV-25 |
| Expected landing time and lateness | Delivery Expectation Standard | LH-18 |
| Repairing a bad night | Feed Re-run Procedure | RP-22 |
| Copying output off-platform | Off-platform Copy Policy | EG-24 |
| Legal instrument behind a copy | Data Sharing Agreement Register | SA-27 |

Everything below is drawn from those recorded standards. Where the recorded material does not settle something this feed needs, that is stated in place and repeated in **Open items** at the end.

## 2. Naming the feed and its output

A feed's name is its contract with everyone who schedules against it. Names follow **pattern FN-13**: the subject first, then the grain of the records, joined with a dash. `parcel-events` is the model — subject `parcel`, grain `events`.

- **Feed name:** `invoice-adjustments` — subject `invoice`, grain `adjustments`. This conforms to FN-13 as given, and needs no adjustment to be onboarded.
- **Output name:** the output carries the feed's name. A consumer must never need a lookup table to connect the feed to its output, so the output is named `invoice-adjustments` and not some separate or derived label.

### Renames

If `invoice-adjustments` is ever renamed:

1. The rename runs through an **alias period**. The old name keeps working throughout.
2. Registered consumers move over during that period.
3. The alias is retired only when the delivery records show **no reads against it** — not on a calendar date, and not on assurances that consumers have migrated.

Renaming without the alias period is not a rename. It is treated as decommissioning one feed and launching another, with every obligation that carries.

## 3. Where the output lands and how the area is organized

The landing area is organized by **layout LZ-14**:

- **One prefix per feed.** `invoice-adjustments` owns exactly one prefix in the landing area, named for the feed.
- **Everything the feed writes lands under that prefix**, partitioned by **write date**.
- **Nothing writes outside its own prefix.** If `invoice-adjustments` turns out to need a second area, that is not a second prefix — under LZ-14 it is two feeds, each named and onboarded in its own right.
- **Nothing but the feed writes inside the prefix.** The point of the layout is that ownership of any object in the zone is readable from its path alone.

### Consumer conduct

Consumers of `invoice-adjustments` **read from the prefix only**. They do not write markers, checkpoints, or scratch output into it. Consumer state lives with the consumer. This should be stated to every consumer at the point they register against the feed, because a consumer writing a checkpoint into the prefix breaks the path-implies-ownership property for everyone.

### Not determined

The recorded layout standard describes the structure of the landing area but not its concrete location. The storage root or URI the prefix sits under, the partition-key spelling and date format used for the write-date partitioning, and the file format and schema of the output are not recorded in the material available. These must be taken from the platform storage owners and from the existing `parcel-events` prefix as it actually stands, and matched exactly.

## 4. Storage registration and how long output lives

Every feed registers its output in **exactly one storage tier**, and the tier decides the output's lifetime.

- **Tier:** `invoice-adjustments` registers in **tier ST-16**, the tier for nightly operational feeds. `parcel-events` sits in ST-16, and the standard states directly that a feed operated like it registers there too.
- **Lifetime:** output in ST-16 is **purged 47 days after its write date**. This is per-partition against that partition's own write date, which matters for re-runs — see §6, where a repaired partition keeps its original write date and therefore its original purge date.
- **Keeping anything longer is not a feed-team decision.** Retaining output beyond 47 days is a **re-registration into a retention tier**, reviewed by the register's owners. The `invoice-adjustments` team cannot grant itself a longer lifetime, and should not design consumers or downstream processes that quietly assume one.

### Capacity behind the registration

Registration is also where capacity is accounted for. Platform storage is bought ahead under a standing vendor commitment, so registering `invoice-adjustments` **draws against line PV-25**, the standing commitment for bulk storage held in the Procurement Commitment Ledger by the procurement office.

What this obliges for onboarding:

1. **Registering the feed is what makes the draw visible to procurement.** There is no separate notification step — but equally, an unregistered or late-registered feed is capacity the renewal will not cover. An unrecorded draw is invisible to the office's renewal sizing.
2. **New draws are confirmed with the vendor manager before they begin.** The `invoice-adjustments` draw must be confirmed with the vendor manager ahead of the feed first writing, not after.
3. **A draw that would take line PV-25 past its committed volume waits for the renewal** rather than assuming headroom exists.
4. **A large draw needs a cycle's notice.** Teams planning a large draw talk to the procurement office a cycle ahead. Renewals run on the office's own negotiation calendar, which the feed team does not control and cannot compress.

### Not determined

The expected nightly and steady-state volume of `invoice-adjustments` output is not recorded, so whether this draw is "large" in PV-25 terms, and whether current PV-25 headroom accommodates it, cannot be determined here. Both must be settled with the procurement office and the vendor manager before the feed begins writing.

## 5. When the feed is expected to land, and repeated lateness

Every nightly feed **declares its expected landing hour in table LH-18**, and that declaration is what consumers schedule against. An undeclared feed has no lateness — only unpredictability. So declaring the hour for `invoice-adjustments` in LH-18 is a hard prerequisite of onboarding, not a follow-up task: until it is declared, consumers have nothing legitimate to schedule against and the feed cannot be said to be late or on time at all.

### How lateness is handled

- A run of `invoice-adjustments` landing **after its declared hour is late**.
- Lateness is tracked **per morning**, against the declaration.
- **One late morning is noted.** No escalation.
- **Repeated late mornings in the same week are raised with the owning team as a delivery matter.** The outcome is one of exactly two things: either the window genuinely moves and **the declaration in LH-18 is corrected**, or **the cause is fixed** and the declared hour stands.
- **Quietly re-declaring a later hour to absorb lateness is not an option.** Moving the declared hour is a change consumers must be told about like any other change to the feed.

### Not determined

The landing hour to declare for `invoice-adjustments` is not recorded and cannot be inferred — it depends on when this feed's upstream inputs are complete (see §6), which is also unrecorded. The owning team for `invoice-adjustments` is likewise not recorded; the material names several operating groups across other pipelines (ingestion duty group, stream operations group, reporting platform team, data services desk, integrations crew, warehouse platform team) but nothing ties any of them to this feed. Repeated-lateness escalation has no addressee until an owning team is named.

## 6. Re-running after a bad night

**A re-run repairs a bad night by replacing it, never by appending to it.** This is the whole of the rule and the source of everything else in **procedure RP-22**.

### The procedure

1. **Wait for the upstream to drain for the affected window.** Re-runs happen *after* the upstream collectors have drained for the window being repaired. Re-running ahead of the upstream repair simply reproduces the bad night.
2. **Replace the affected write-date partitions whole.** Not a merge, not an append, not a patch of the bad records — the partition is replaced in its entirety.
3. **Write under the feed's own prefix.** The repair goes to the `invoice-adjustments` prefix, the same one as normal operation. LZ-14 applies to re-runs exactly as it applies to nightly runs.
4. **The original write date stays the partition's identity.** A re-run performed days later still lands under the night it repairs. Consumers re-reading that partition see the corrected records exactly where the bad ones were.

### The hard boundary

A re-run that would change a partition's write date **is not a re-run**. It is a new feed writing into an old feed's zone, and the layout forbids it. If a repair cannot preserve the original write date, it is not covered by RP-22 and must not be performed as one.

Note the interaction with §4: because a repaired partition keeps its original write date, it also keeps its original ST-16 purge date. A partition repaired on day 40 is still purged on day 47 from the *original* night, not 47 days from the repair.

### What a re-run cannot fix

The model feed makes the limit explicit, and it carries directly: `parcel-events` runs only after its collectors drain, and a **missing hour in the output is a collector matter, not a feed matter** — re-running the feed cannot supply records a collector never delivered. The same reasoning applies to `invoice-adjustments`: if its upstream never delivered records for a window, no re-run produces them. The fix belongs upstream, and only then does a re-run of `invoice-adjustments` make sense.

### Not determined

The specific upstream that `invoice-adjustments` runs behind — the counterpart to the parcel collectors — is not recorded. Both the run gating in §5 (when it is safe for the feed to start) and step 1 of this procedure (when it is safe to re-run) depend on knowing what that upstream is and how its drain is observed. This must be established before the feed goes live, since without it there is no way to distinguish a feed fault from an upstream shortfall.

## 7. If output is ever copied outside the platform

**No feed output leaves the platform on an operator's judgment alone.** This is not the operator's call for `parcel-events` and it is not the operator's call for `invoice-adjustments`.

### The EG-24 approval

Every copy outside the platform carries an **EG-24 approval** naming three things:

1. **The receiving party**
2. **The purpose**
3. **The date the copy will be deleted**

An approval missing any of the three is **returned unactioned**. The approval is **filed before the copy is made**, not alongside it and not after.

**Re-copies** under an existing approval are re-copies only while **the purpose and the recipient are unchanged**. A different recipient, or the same recipient for a different purpose, is a new copy needing its own approval.

### The covering instrument

An EG-24 approval must also **cite the agreement that makes the transfer lawful**. The covering instrument is looked up in the **Data Sharing Agreement Register**, maintained by the legal office — the register is the **only authoritative list**, and copies of instruments held by teams are working copies whose dates do not govern.

Each instrument is registered as an **SA-27 entry** carrying:

- the counterparty
- the categories of records covered
- the permitted purposes
- the instrument's expiry

The citation is **checked against the entry's categories and purposes, not against the transferring team's intent**. A good-faith reading by the `invoice-adjustments` team of what an instrument "obviously covers" carries no weight against what the entry actually says.

**A transfer with no instrument to cite does not proceed, whatever its purpose.** An expired or absent instrument means the transfer waits for the legal office, however routine the request.

### Not determined

Whether any existing SA-27 entry covers invoice-adjustment records as a category is not recorded and is not something this document can determine — the register is authoritative and held by the legal office. If any off-platform sharing of `invoice-adjustments` output is anticipated, the covering instrument must be confirmed with the legal office in advance, because the absence of one blocks the transfer outright rather than delaying it.

## 8. Onboarding checklist

Ordered so the blocking prerequisites come first:

1. Confirm the feed name `invoice-adjustments` against FN-13 — subject then grain, dash-joined. *(Conforms as given.)*
2. Name the owning team, and record it. Required before lateness escalation under LH-18 has an addressee.
3. Identify the upstream this feed runs behind and how its drain is observed. Required before both the landing hour and the re-run procedure are operable.
4. Create the single landing-zone prefix named `invoice-adjustments`, partitioned by write date, matching the concrete root, partition spelling, and format of the existing `parcel-events` prefix.
5. Register the output in **tier ST-16** — one tier, 47-day purge from write date.
6. Confirm the resulting **PV-25** draw with the vendor manager before the feed first writes; if the draw is large, engage the procurement office a cycle ahead of the renewal.
7. Declare the expected landing hour in **table LH-18**. The feed should not be presented to consumers before this exists.
8. Register consumers against the declared hour, and tell them the prefix is read-only to them — no markers, checkpoints, or scratch output.
9. Brief operators on **RP-22**: replace whole partitions, preserve the original write date, and only after the upstream has drained for the affected window.
10. Brief operators on **EG-24 / SA-27**: no off-platform copy without a prior approval naming recipient, purpose and deletion date, citing a live register instrument that covers the record category.

## Open items

The following are things this document needs and that the available material does not settle. Each must be resolved with the named holder before `invoice-adjustments` goes live.

2. **The upstream `invoice-adjustments` runs behind, and how its drain is observed.** Not recorded. `parcel-events` runs only after its parcel collectors drain; the counterpart for this feed is unknown. This blocks both the nightly run gating and step 1 of the RP-22 re-run procedure, and without it a feed fault cannot be distinguished from an upstream shortfall.
3. **The expected landing hour to declare in table LH-18.** Not recorded and not inferable — it depends on item 2. Until declared, the feed has no lateness, only unpredictability.
4. **The concrete landing-zone location.** LZ-14 gives the structure (one prefix per feed, partitioned by write date) but no storage root or URI. No storage connections are configured on this platform to read it from. Take it from the existing `parcel-events` prefix.
5. **Partition-key spelling and write-date format.** Not recorded. Must match `parcel-events` exactly.
6. **Output file format and record schema.** Not recorded for this feed or for `parcel-events`.
7. **Expected output volume, and PV-25 headroom.** Not recorded. Determines whether the draw is "large" (needing a cycle's notice to the procurement office) and whether the line has committed volume to absorb it. Confirm with the procurement office and vendor manager.
8. **Whether any SA-27 instrument covers invoice-adjustment records.** Not recorded, and only the legal office's register is authoritative. Needed only if off-platform sharing is anticipated — but if it is, the absence of a covering instrument blocks the transfer entirely.
9. **The mechanism behind "delivery records" and consumer registration.** FN-13 retires a rename alias when delivery records show no reads, and LH-18 tracks lateness per morning against the declaration; neither the system holding those records nor the consumer registry is identified in the available material.

# Change Plan — Adding a Field to `orders-ledger` Records

**Stream:** orders-ledger (governed tier)
**Change type:** addition of a new field to the record shape
**Prepared:** 2026-08-10
**Audience:** the stream's owning team, executing end to end

---

## 1. What governs this change

`orders-ledger` carries the order lifecycle records every revenue report is built from, and its records feed the statutory accounts. Because of that it is a **governed-tier** stream: how it changes is bound by *Governed Tier Obligations*, not by the producing team's own judgment (*Orders Ledger Stream Runbook*).

Five instruments bind this specific change, and none of them is optional:

| Instrument | What it fixes | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Class RB-7** | A field added to a record shape is an *incompatible* change; consumers are owed **17 business days** of advance notice before it is applied | *Change Class Directory* |
| **Mode CM-3** | The orders stream's compatibility mode — the strictest. A new version must be readable by every consumer of the previous one **without a code change** | *Schema Version Register* |
| **Bulletin AN-5** | The only channel for the consumer-facing notice; issued centrally, not by the producing team | *Change Announcement Directory* |
| **Window QW-4** | The quiet window from journal cutoff to statement sign-off; production alterations to systems whose figures flow into the statements wait until the books are signed | *Company Close Calendar* |
| **Form AT-12** | The owner's personal attestation that closes the change after it is live | *Attestation Procedure* |

Two constraints sit above all of them:

- **Classification happens before any work begins**, and *the owner cannot waive a classification* (*Governed Tier Obligations*).
- **A record shape that reaches the stream unregistered is an incident, not a shortcut** (*Schema Version Register*).

### The central design constraint: RB-7 and CM-3 together

These two are not in conflict, but they are easy to misread as one rule. RB-7 sets what the change *owes consumers* (notice); CM-3 sets whether the new version *may be registered at all*. A field addition is RB-7 regardless of how small the producer thinks it is — "the class does not shorten for changes the producer considers small: compatibility is judged from the consumer's side." Separately, at registration time the proposed version is checked against CM-3, and it fails that check unless every consumer of the current version can read the new version without changing their code.

**Practical consequence: design the field so that it is additive and ignorable by every existing reader before you propose it.** A field that forces any registered consumer to change code cannot be registered on this stream, and the change stops there — the notice period is irrelevant if the version cannot be registered.

---

## 2. Execution sequence

Steps are ordered by dependency. The letters in brackets are the approvals catalogued in §3.

### Phase 0 — Standing checks (before any work)

**Step 0.1 — Confirm the owner's seat is filled.**
The AT-12 signature is personal to the producing service's named owner and cannot be delegated below that role, and *"a vacancy in that role suspends changes rather than the attestation."* If the owner role is vacant, the change does not start. Fill the seat first.

**Step 0.2 — Read the current register entry.**
Pull the stream's entry from the *Schema Version Register*: current version, the classification of the change that produced it, and who approved it. This entry is the baseline the new version is checked against, and it is also where the AN-5 bulletin will be posted.

**Step 0.3 — Pull the consumer list from the agreement ledger.**
Every consuming team registers a **CA-9** agreement per stream, naming the consuming service, its owner, and **the fields it depends on** (*Consumer Agreement Ledger*). This list is the notice boundary and the CM-3 evidence base in one. Extract, for each registered consumer: service, owner, declared fields.

> Note the ledger's hard edge: *"a team that never registered is owed nothing, however long it has been reading."* Unregistered readers are outside this plan's notice obligations. If you know of readers who never registered, the correct action is to get them to register — not to extend notice to them informally, and not to skip a step because you believe they exist.

### Phase 1 — Proposal and classification

**Step 1.1 — Write the proposal against the registered schema.**
Per the *Orders Ledger Stream Runbook*, any change to the record shape "starts with a proposal against the stream's registered schema." The proposal must carry, at minimum, what the downstream instruments will demand of it later:

- the new field: name, type, nullability, default/absence behaviour, and semantics;
- the current registered version it is proposed against, and the proposed new version;
- the CM-3 argument (Step 2.1);
- the change class (Step 1.2);
- the scope statement that AT-12 will later be signed against — because attestation asserts *"the announced scope is the delivered scope,"* the scope you write here is the scope you are bound to deliver, no more and no less.

**Step 1.2 — Classify the change as RB-7. [A]**
Adding a field to the record shape is class RB-7 (*Change Class Directory*, *Governed Tier Obligations*). Record the classification in the proposal. Do this **before any implementation work begins** — the classification gate is on the start of work, not on deployment. The owner may not waive it, and may not argue it down on grounds of the field being small or optional.

If anyone proposes a lighter class (on the theory that a pure addition is a "compatible addition"), the directory's tiebreak governs: *"When in doubt between two classes, the heavier one applies until the owner of the consuming side agrees otherwise in writing."* A downgrade therefore requires the *consuming-side owner's written agreement* — see §3[F] and the caution in §4.

### Phase 2 — Design for CM-3

**Step 2.1 — Build the compatibility argument, consumer by consumer.**
Using the CA-9 declared-field lists from Step 0.3, show for each registered consumer that it can read the new version without a code change. Absence of a per-consumer argument is absence of a CM-3 case.

**Step 2.2 — Adjust the field design until the argument holds.**
If any registered consumer would need a code change, the version fails the CM-3 check at registration. Redesign — or, where the consumer must change, sequence their change ahead of registration and record it in their CA-9 agreement. Do not carry an unresolved consumer into registration.

**Step 2.3 — If consumer-side testing needs sample records off the platform. [E]**
No feed output leaves the platform on an operator's judgment alone. Any copy outside the platform carries an **EG-24** approval naming the receiving party, the purpose, and the date the copy will be deleted — *an approval missing any of the three is returned unactioned* — and the approval is **filed before the copy is made**. The approval must also cite the covering instrument that makes the transfer lawful, looked up in the legal office's list; *a transfer with no instrument to cite does not proceed, whatever its purpose* (*Off-platform Copy Policy*). Keeping all validation on-platform avoids this step entirely; prefer that.

### Phase 3 — Register the new version

**Step 3.1 — Submit the version to the register and pass the CM-3 check. [B]**
The version is checked against CM-3 at registration time. Registration must complete **before any producer writes the new shape** — this ordering is absolute, and violating it converts the change into an incident (§6).

**Step 3.2 — Confirm the entry is complete.**
The resulting entry must carry the version, the classification of the change that produced it (RB-7), and who approved it. The entry is the authoritative answer to "what changed and when," and the AN-5 bulletin will be posted against it, so it must exist and be correct before Phase 4.

### Phase 4 — Announce

**Step 4.1 — Request the AN-5 bulletin from the central announcing function.**
*"Nothing is announced by the producing team directly"* (*Orders Ledger Stream Runbook*); notices are issued centrally *"so no consumer's notice depends on which team is making the change"* (*Change Announcement Directory*). The owning team supplies the content; it does not send the notice.

**Step 4.2 — Deliver to every consumer on the agreement ledger.**
The bulletin goes to *every* consumer the stream's CA-9 ledger lists — including those whose declared fields are untouched. The discretion the ledger grants (Step 5.2) is about *waiting*, not about *notifying*.

**Step 4.3 — Post the bulletin against the stream's register entry.**
The posted copy is the authoritative one: *"the authoritative copy when a delivered copy and the register disagree."* If a consumer later disputes what was announced, the register entry is what settles it.

**Step 4.4 — File the bulletin under RR-21 with its delivery evidence, at issue. [D]**
Issued bulletins are corporate correspondence under series **RR-21** and are *"filed with their delivery evidence at the time of issue — filing is part of issuing, not an afterthought."* Retention length and disposal belong to the records office, not to the announcing or owning team. The delivery evidence is not merely a filing formality: it is what establishes the date the notice clock starts from.

**Step 4.5 — Record the delivery date.**
The RB-7 notice period *"runs from the day the announcement is actually delivered"* — not the day it was drafted, approved, or posted. Take the delivery date from the RR-21 delivery evidence.

### Phase 5 — Serve the notice period

**Step 5.1 — Count 17 business days from delivery.**
Seventeen business days of advance notice, *"counted in the consuming teams' working calendar"* — the consumers' calendar, not the producer's. Where consumers sit on different working calendars, the period must be satisfied for each of them; in practice, count against the latest-finishing calendar among registered consumers.

**Step 5.2 — Review the agreements and decide who you must wait for.**
*"Agreements are reviewed when a stream's shape changes: a consumer whose declared fields are untouched by a change may be notified without being waited for, at the announcing owner's discretion"* (*Consumer Agreement Ledger*). Work through the CA-9 list and mark each consumer as *touched* or *untouched* by this change.

Read this carefully against RB-7, which says the class *does not shorten* and that compatibility is judged from the consumer's side. The two reconcile as: RB-7 fixes the class and its 17-day obligation to consumers of the stream; the ledger's discretion determines which registered consumers that waiting obligation is owed to individually. **Whether that discretion can empty the waiting period entirely for a pure addition — where by construction no declared field is touched — is not settled by the material available.** See Open items. The conservative execution, and the one consistent with the directory's "heavier class applies" tiebreak, is to serve the full 17 business days and use the discretion only to avoid blocking on individual non-responsive untouched consumers.

**Step 5.3 — Handle consumer responses during the period.**
A consumer who reports during the notice period that they *cannot* read the new version without a code change has contradicted the CM-3 case. Stop, return to Phase 2, and re-register — compatibility is judged from the consumer's side, so their assessment governs over the producer's.

### Phase 6 — Schedule the apply

**Step 6.1 — Check the close calendar's current standing.**
Change timing *"does not belong to the producing team alone."* Period dates, cutoff times, and the current window's standing are published on the finance group's internal page each period (*Company Close Calendar*). Read that page for the period you intend to apply in — do not schedule from memory of last period's dates.

**Step 6.2 — Schedule the apply outside QW-4.**
QW-4 runs from journal cutoff to statement sign-off. `orders-ledger` feeds the statutory accounts, so it is squarely within *"systems whose figures flow into the statements"*: production alterations wait until the books are signed. The apply date must fall outside QW-4 **and** on or after the end of the 17-business-day notice period — whichever is later governs.

**Step 6.3 — Only if the apply genuinely cannot wait: seek a written QW-4 exception. [C]**
The controller's office grants exceptions in writing, and *"treats them as findings in the close report."* An exception is a cost, not a bypass; a field addition will rarely justify one.

### Phase 7 — Apply

**Step 7.1 — Cut the producer over to the registered shape.**
The producer writes the registered version and nothing else. Any deviation between what is written and what is registered — an extra field, a different type, a renamed field — is an unregistered shape reaching the stream, i.e. an incident (§6).

**Step 7.2 — Watch the overnight settle and the morning lag review.**
The stream settles during the overnight window and its lag is reviewed each morning (*Orders Ledger Stream Runbook*). The first settle after the apply is both the operational check and the precondition for attestation.

### Phase 8 — Close the change

**Step 8.1 — Wait for the first full settlement to pass.**
AT-12 is filed *"once the change is live and the first full settlement has passed"* — not at deploy time.

**Step 8.2 — File form AT-12. [G]**
The producing service's named owner personally signs that:

1. the records now flowing match the registered version;
2. no consumer-visible field was dropped along the way;
3. the announced scope is the delivered scope.

The signature *cannot be delegated below the service's named owner*. Assemble the evidence for each of the three assertions before signing: (1) against the register entry from Step 3.2, (2) against the pre-change field list from Step 0.2, (3) against the AN-5 bulletin as posted in Step 4.3.

**Step 8.3 — Do not leave the form unfiled.**
*"An unattested change stays open in the tier's books and is raised at every review until the form is filed."* There is no expiry on this; time does not close the change.

### Phase 9 — After the change

**Step 9.1 — Update CA-9 agreements as consumers adopt the field.**
The agreement names the fields the consuming service depends on. A consumer that begins depending on the new field must have it in their declared fields — otherwise the next change to that field will treat them as untouched and may not wait for them.

**Step 9.2 — Confirm the register entry and the posted bulletin are the record.**
These are what the next operator, the next auditor, and the next change will read. Nothing in this plan's working papers substitutes for them.

---

## 3. Approvals this change needs

| # | Approval | Who grants it | When | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | **Change classification as RB-7** | Set by the *Change Class Directory*; recorded by the owner | Before any work begins | Not an approval the owner can waive or downgrade unilaterally |
| **B** | **Schema version registration** (CM-3 check passed; approver recorded in the entry) | Not determined — see Open items | Before any producer writes the shape | The entry records "who approved it," so an approver exists; the material does not name the role |
| **C** | **QW-4 exception** — *conditional, only if the apply must fall inside the quiet window* | The controller's office, in writing | Before scheduling inside QW-4 | Recorded as a finding in the close report |
| **D** | **RR-21 filing of the bulletin with delivery evidence** | Records management office holds the series; issuing team files at issue | At the moment of issue | Disposal is reviewed by the records office, never the issuing team |
| **E** | **EG-24 off-platform copy approval** — *conditional, only if sample records leave the platform* | Not determined — see Open items | Filed before the copy is made | Must name receiving party, purpose, and deletion date, and cite a covering instrument from the legal office's list |
| **F** | **Written agreement from the consuming-side owner** — *conditional, only if a lighter class than RB-7 is argued* | The owner of the consuming side | Before relying on the lighter class | The directory's tiebreak: the heavier class applies until this is in writing |
| **G** | **AT-12 attestation** | The producing service's named owner, personally | After the change is live and the first full settlement has passed | Non-delegable; a vacancy suspends changes rather than the attestation |

---

## 4. Rules that constrain *when* the change may be applied

1. **Not before registration.** The version is registered before any producer writes it. No exception is described; the alternative is an incident.
2. **Not before the 17th business day** after the AN-5 bulletin was *delivered*, counted in the consuming teams' working calendar. The clock starts at delivery, not at drafting, approval, or posting.
3. **Not inside QW-4** — the stretch from journal cutoff to statement sign-off in the current period — unless the controller's office has granted a written exception, which is logged as a close-report finding.
4. **Not while the owner role is vacant.** A vacancy in the named owner role suspends changes.
5. **Not on a shortened clock because the change looks small.** RB-7 does not shorten for changes the producer considers minor; compatibility is judged from the consumer's side.
6. **Not on a lighter class by the producer's own reading.** Between two candidate classes, the heavier applies until the consuming-side owner agrees otherwise in writing.
7. **Not beyond the announced scope.** AT-12 asserts that announced scope equals delivered scope. Expanding the change after the bulletin is issued means re-announcing and re-serving the notice period, not quietly widening the deploy.

---

## 5. What consumers are owed, in order

| When | What is owed | To whom |
|---|---|---|
| At issue | An **AN-5 bulletin**, issued centrally rather than by the producing team | Every consumer listed in the stream's CA-9 agreement ledger |
| At issue | The bulletin **posted against the register entry** — the authoritative copy in any dispute with a delivered copy | All consumers, as the reference of record |
| At issue | The bulletin **filed under RR-21 with its delivery evidence** | The firm's records; consumers rely on it for the notice start date |
| From delivery | **17 business days** before the change is applied, counted in the consuming teams' working calendar | Consumers of the stream — see §5.2 on the untouched-fields discretion |
| During the shape change | **A review of their CA-9 agreement** against the change | Each registered consumer |
| After the change | An owner attestation (AT-12) that no consumer-visible field was dropped and the delivered scope matches what was announced | Consumers, via the tier's books |

Explicitly **not** owed anything: teams reading the stream without a registered CA-9 agreement, *"however long it has been reading."* Registration is a condition of read access and is the notice boundary.

---

## 6. If it goes wrong

**Unregistered shape reaches the stream.** This is an incident by definition, not a variance to be documented after the fact (*Schema Version Register*).

**Severity and escalation.** Severity is assigned when the record is opened and *"belongs to the standard, not to the team that opened it."* A reconciliation or settlement control failing across a statement cycle is band **SB-8**, which notifies the owning team and the platform group's shift lead at opening and escalates along the **garnet route**: platform shift lead → duty manager → head of platform operations, one rung at a time, never skipping a rung that has acknowledged. Each rung holds for the acknowledgment clock recorded in the clocks table (not in the roster). Single-night failures and non-control degradations carry lighter bands that notify the owning team only and do not escalate unattended (*Incident Severity Standard*, *Escalation Roster*).

**If the failure falls inside a statutory filing window,** notification additionally follows the compliance office's schedule — that obligation is not the engineering organization's to schedule.

**Closing out.** A closed control-failure incident files a **PM-6** review record: a timeline of the nights in question, the originating conditions as actually understood, the corrections to be made each with a named owner, and the review meeting's outcome. A record whose corrections have no owner is returned rather than filed. Hours spent on the nights in question are entered in the workforce office's ledger *before* the record is filed (*Review Record Standard*).

**Note on rollback:** the material available does not describe a backout procedure for a governed-stream schema change — no rule was found on reverting to the previous registered version, nor on whether a revert is itself a registrable change requiring its own RB-7 notice. See Open items.

---
